analysis.one_liner: Allows Americans to buy lower-priced prescription drugs from Canada and other approved countries.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: referred to a House subcommittee in March 2005, it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2007, with 22 bipartisan cosponsors and no floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed federal law to let pharmacies, wholesalers, and individuals import prescription drugs from Canada, Australia, Japan, New Zealand, Switzerland, and European Union countries, where the same medicines often sell for far less. It required those importers and exporters to register with the FDA, submit to inspections, verify the chain of custody of each drug, and post bonds, and it barred drug makers from punishing or cutting off anyone who imported. The bill was introduced by Representative Jo Ann Emerson, a Republican from Missouri, with 22 cosponsors from both parties, and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who fill prescriptions, especially seniors and people without generous insurance, who pay among the highest brand-drug prices in the world. The bill's own findings estimated that opening the market could save consumers at least $38 billion a year, and that Americans pay up to five times what consumers in other countries pay for the same medicines. Pharmacies, wholesalers, and licensed foreign pharmacies would gain a new legal business channel.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans who fill prescriptions, especially seniors

how_it_helps.text: Waives the federal restriction that blocks importation of prescription drugs exported from the United States, letting qualifying drugs flow back in at foreign prices.
Permits individuals to import up to a 90-day personal supply from registered exporters with a valid prescription, and lets pharmacies and wholesalers import commercially.

The bill's findings state Americans pay up to 5 times more for prescriptions than consumers in other countries and that open pharmaceutical markets could save American consumers at least $38 billion each year.

Prohibits manufacturers from discriminating against registered importers and exporters by charging them higher prices, cutting off supplies, or refusing to do business with them, and makes clear that reselling in the U.S. a drug properly sold abroad is not patent infringement.
Requires the FDA to publish a public list of registered exporters on its website and a toll-free number, so consumers know which sellers are vetted.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would face competition from their own products sold at lower prices abroad and would lose their ability to charge U.S. patients much more for the same medicine. The FDA and Customs would take on new inspection costs, though the bill covers those through fees on importers and exporters, and manufacturers could pass along new filing fees.

drawbacks.text: The bill excludes entire categories of medicines from importation, including biological products such as monoclonal antibodies, injected and infused drugs, controlled substances, and drugs inhaled during surgery, so patients on those treatments would see no savings.

Manufacturers are not compelled to sell a drug in any country, so a company could simply stop distributing a medicine in Canada or other permitted countries to cut off the supply available for import, a loophole the bill explicitly leaves open.

The safety machinery is heavy: exporters must post bonds of up to $1 million, importers and exporters pay registration and inspection fees capped at 1 percent of imported drug value, and the FDA must inspect facilities at least 12 times a year, compliance costs that would be built into the price of imported drugs.

Opponents of drug importation have long argued that foreign-sourced medicines raise counterfeit and safety risks; the bill responds with chain-of-custody verification and track-and-trace requirements, but the inspection regime would still depend on FDA capacity that critics said was insufficient.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large and concrete: cheaper versions of the same FDA-approved medicines, with the bill's findings pegging annual consumer savings at $38 billion or more. The costs fall almost entirely on drug makers, plus compliance overhead that would trim but not erase the savings for consumers. The most serious design weakness is that manufacturers could legally avoid the law by withdrawing products from permitted countries, and whole classes of drugs are excluded, so the savings would reach many but not all patients.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Representative Jo Ann Emerson of Missouri introduced the Pharmaceutical Market Access and Drug Safety Act of 2005 on February 9, 2005, joined by original cosponsors including Representatives Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced.
On March 14, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was taken.
The bill gathered 22 cosponsors, 18 Democrats, 3 Republicans, and 1 Independent, but never received a markup, a floor vote, or a Senate companion vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off because the bill died: they kept the ability to charge U.S. patients far higher prices than consumers abroad pay for the same medicines. Committee leadership also benefited, in that the House never had to take a recorded position on a consumer issue with bipartisan appeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept charging U.S. prices

for.name: Rep. Jo Ann Emerson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled a bipartisan group of original cosponsors.

for.name: Rep. Sherrod Brown of Ohio and other cosponsors
for.role: 18 Democratic, 3 Republican, and 1 Independent House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total support to 22 members across both parties.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; chaired by Rep. Joe Barton (R-TX) in the 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or a vote; it sat in the Subcommittee on Health from March 2005 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers (PhRMA and member companies)
against.what_they_did: Opposed prescription drug importation legislation, which would have ended the practice of charging U.S. patients higher prices than consumers abroad for the same drugs.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican and the 22 cosponsors split 18 Democrats, 3 Republicans, and 1 Independent, so support crossed party lines; the bill's fate was decided in committee, not by a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would have forced them to compete with their own products sold at lower prices in Canada, Europe, and other permitted countries, and barred them from discriminating against or cutting off importers. The industry's higher U.S. prices are the direct cost to American patients, which is why its interest runs against the public's in this bill.

industries.industry: Licensed foreign pharmacies, wholesale importers, and internet pharmacies
industries.note: The bill creates a permanent legal channel for drug importation, but only through FDA-registered pharmacies, wholesalers, and exporters that pass inspections and pay fees, effectively licensing a new industry with a protected gatekeeping role.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers
industries.note: The bill expressly preserves manufacturers' freedom to give rebate discounts to insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, and 340B covered entities without sharing those discounts with importers, keeping the existing rebate system intact even as it opens retail importation.
